lines.text: [curious] One and a half percent back, on everything. [pause] So who pays for that?
Say you spend a hundred dollars. The store keeps about ninety-seven sixty. The rest is the swipe fee.
About two dollars goes to the bank that issued your card. Fourteen cents to Visa or Mastercard. And about a quarter to the store's payment processor.
Your bank pays you a dollar fifty of its two dollars. That leaves about fifty cents, before its costs.
[serious] The real money is interest. Nearly half of cardholders carry a balance at times, at around twenty-two percent a year.
So who funds your rewards? Every shopper, through prices that include card fees, and everyone who carries a balance.
The bank that issues your card earns the most, and carries the risk. Visa and Mastercard take a small toll on every swipe. Amex and Discover do both.
A debit card lends you nothing. And U.S. law caps big banks' debit fees at about twenty-seven cents on a hundred-dollar purchase, so debit rarely pays rewards.
Phone wallets swap the plastic for a token. But the payment still runs on the same networks, with the same fees.
The bigger threat is cheap public payment rails, like Brazil's Pix and India's UPI, and maybe a digital euro. They skip the card networks entirely.
So, will credit cards survive? Probably. People still borrow, and chase rewards. But cheaper rails squeeze swipe fees, and swipe fees pay your cash back.
[upbeat] Every frame of this film is code: Tabbied patterns, rendered with Remotion.
